# Technical Brief: Optimizing Compiler Internals

## 1. SSA Construction

**Dominance-frontier-based construction (Cytron–Ferrante–Rosen–Wegman–Zadeck, 1991).** This is the classical algorithm. It first computes the dominator tree (efficiently via the **Lengauer–Tarjan algorithm**, near-linear time using path compression on a union-find-like structure over the CFG's depth-first spanning tree). From the dominator tree it computes **dominance frontiers**: the dominance frontier of node `n`, DF(n), is the set of nodes `m` such that `n` dominates a predecessor of `m` but does not strictly dominate `m` itself. Phi-nodes are placed at the iterated dominance frontier of the set of definition sites for each variable: whenever a variable is defined in block `n`, a phi is inserted at every block in DF(n), and since inserting a phi is itself a new definition, the process iterates to a fixpoint (iterated dominance frontier, DF+). This guarantees **semi-pruned SSA** (phi insertion limited to variables live across blocks) or, with a prior liveness pass, **pruned SSA** (no dead phis). Renaming is performed by a dominator-tree preorder walk with a per-variable stack: pushing a new SSA name at each definition, using the stack top at each use, and popping on exit from the subtree, which gives each use the correct reaching definition because of the dominance property (every use is dominated by its definition in valid SSA).

**Braun et al.'s simple and efficient SSA construction (2013).** This avoids computing dominance frontiers at all. It builds SSA directly during a single pass over the CFG (even abstract-syntax-tree-driven, without a pre-built CFG) using **local value numbering** per block plus a **predecessor-based recursive lookup**: a use with no local definition recursively queries each predecessor block for its reaching definition, inserting a phi if there is more than one predecessor and memoizing it immediately to break cycles in loops (an "incomplete phi" placeholder is used until all predecessors are known, important for blocks that are not yet sealed because not all predecessors have been processed, e.g. loop headers). After construction, a separate **phi-simplification pass** removes trivially redundant phis (phis with all identical operands, or self-referential phis) to approach minimal SSA. This method trades a bit of extra minimality-pass work for much simpler implementation and is used in libFirm and in several JIT IRs (e.g. early work predating this is similar to the approach used by Cliff Click's sea-of-nodes construction in the HotSpot C2 compiler, which builds SSA lazily with the same "incomplete phi, seal predecessors" idea).

**SSA destruction and the lost-copy/swap problems.** Converting back to non-SSA form (needed before most register allocators or machine-code emission) requires replacing phis with explicit copies on predecessor edges. Naively placing a copy for each phi operand at the end of each predecessor block is unsound in the presence of **parallel copy semantics**: if two phis in the same block must simultaneously swap values that were computed via sequential copies, a naive sequentialization corrupts one value (the **swap problem**), and if a live range is overwritten by a copy inserted on a critical edge before the use it was meant to feed, you get the **lost-copy problem**. The standard fix (Sreedhar, Ju, Gillies, Santhanam, and later refined approaches) is to treat the operands of each phi plus the phi result as members of **webs** that must be coalesced or carefully live-range-split, inserting copies at points proven safe by a **parallel-copy-to-sequential-copy conversion algorithm** that treats each phi as a parallel-assignment problem (essentially topologically sorting a permutation graph and introducing a temporary to break cycles, like swapping two registers via a scratch register). Critical edges (edges from a block with multiple successors to a block with multiple predecessors) must be split first so copies have a unique safe insertion point.

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's inclusion-based (subset-constraint) points-to analysis.** Each pointer variable `p` is modeled with a points-to set `pts(p)`, and assignments generate subset constraints: `p = q` generates `pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)`; `p = &x` generates `x ∈ pts(p)`; `p = *q` and `*p = q` generate conditional/dereference constraints. These constraints are solved to a fixpoint via a worklist algorithm propagating points-to information along a constraint graph, giving a **flow-insensitive, context-insensitive** but comparatively precise (subset, not unification) analysis. Its worst-case complexity is cubic in program size (O(n³)), which has driven decades of work on sparser/BDD-based implementations (e.g. `bddbddb`) to make it scale.

**Steensgaard's unification-based points-to analysis.** Instead of subset constraints, Steensgaard's analysis unifies the points-to sets of any two variables related by an assignment (using a union-find data structure), so `p = q` merges `pts(p)` and `pts(q)` into one equivalence class rather than keeping them as separate sets related by inclusion. This loses precision — unrelated pointers that are merely assigned to each other become conflated — but achieves near-linear time (O(n·α(n)) with union-find), making it attractive for whole-program analysis in compilers prioritizing compile-time budget over maximal precision.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA).** Used heavily in LLVM and in C/C++ compilers exploiting strict aliasing rules: two memory accesses are assumed non-aliasing if their accessed types are incompatible under the language's aliasing rules (e.g. accessing memory through an `int*` vs a `float*` when the underlying object was never defined to be a union of both). LLVM encodes this as **TBAA metadata** attached to loads/stores, structured as a tree of type descriptors with parent/child relationships representing "may alias if same type or an ancestor type." This is a purely structural, flow- and context-insensitive analysis layered independently from points-to analysis, and it must be disabled/weakened under `-fno-strict-aliasing` or when source language semantics (e.g. Rust's less restrictive raw-pointer rules, or C's `char*` exception) require it.

**Precision/scalability axes.** All real alias analyses are classified along flow-sensitivity (does the points-to set change across program points, i.e. is a separate solution computed per CFG node, as opposed to one global solution), context-sensitivity (are call sites distinguished, e.g. via **k-CFA** — bounding call-string length to depth k — or full call-string approaches that clone analysis state per call chain), field-sensitivity (are struct/object fields distinguished rather than collapsed to one points-to set per aggregate), and heap modeling granularity (allocation-site-based abstract locations vs. fully merged "heap" summary node). LLVM's query interface exposes results via the `AliasResult` lattice: **NoAlias**, **MustAlias**, **MayAlias**, and **PartialAlias**, letting optimization passes (GVN, licm, dse) query precision-appropriate answers without needing to know which underlying analysis (basic alias analysis, TBAA, scoped-noalias metadata, or a custom pass) produced them.

## 3. Register Allocation

**Chaitin–Briggs graph-coloring register allocation.** Build an **interference graph** where nodes are live ranges (or virtual registers) and edges connect any two ranges simultaneously live at some program point; an available coloring with k colors (physical registers) means no two interfering ranges share a register. The classical **Chaitin algorithm** repeatedly removes ("simplifies") nodes of degree < k from the graph onto a stack (guaranteed colorable once replaced), and when no such node exists, picks a node to spill using a spill-cost heuristic (typically (uses+defs weighted by loop nesting depth) / degree) and marks it for spill code insertion, then restarts. **Briggs's optimistic coloring** refinement defers the spill decision: push high-degree nodes onto the stack anyway (optimistically assuming a color will still be free when popped, since not all k neighbors necessarily received distinct colors), only actually spilling if, upon popping, no color remains. Briggs also introduced **conservative coalescing**: merge two move-related nodes only if the resulting merged node still has fewer than k neighbors of significant degree, preventing coalescing from creating new un-colorable nodes (the more aggressive Chaitin-style coalescing can increase spilling).

**Linear scan register allocation (Poletto & Sarkar).** Instead of building a full interference graph, compute **live intervals** (a single contiguous [start,end) range approximation of liveness, assuming each virtual register is defined once and used contiguously, which is why this is commonly paired with SSA or near-SSA IRs) and sort them by start point. Scan intervals in order, maintaining a pool of free physical registers; when an interval starts, assign it a free register, and when active intervals' ends are passed, return their register to the pool. When no register is free, **spill** the active interval with the furthest-away next use (or, in simpler implementations, the one with the lowest priority), which is a much cheaper decision procedure than graph coloring's NP-complete coloring problem but less precise, since linear intervals overapproximate true liveness (gaps in actual use aren't modeled without **live-range splitting**). This is the allocator of choice for JITs needing fast compilation, e.g. early LLVM fast-path backends and various JIT engines, because it runs in near-linear time versus graph coloring's higher practical cost.

**SSA-based (chordal graph) register allocation (Hack, Grund, Goos).** A key theoretical result: the interference graph of a program in strict SSA form is a **chordal graph** (every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord), and chordal graphs are colorable in polynomial time via a **perfect elimination ordering**, in contrast to the general NP-complete graph-coloring problem Chaitin-Briggs must heuristically approximate. This enables an allocator that computes an optimal (for a fixed k, modulo spilling) coloring directly from the SSA dominance structure without the simplify/spill worklist heuristics, then resolves the result into actual machine registers by solving a **"register-register move" puzzle** at block boundaries (since different blocks may have colored the same value differently, requiring parallel-copy resolution much like SSA destruction's swap/lost-copy handling) before finally eliminating the SSA form.

**Supporting mechanisms common across approaches.** **Live-range splitting** breaks one long live range into several shorter ones at profitable program points (e.g. around loop boundaries) so that only the hot portion need occupy a register continuously, reducing spill pressure; **rematerialization** avoids a spill/reload by instead recomputing a cheap value (e.g. a constant or simple address computation) at the use site rather than storing/loading it, when recomputation is cheaper than a memory round-trip; and in linear scan specifically, **second-chance binpacking** allows a previously spilled interval to be re-assigned a register later in its lifetime if one frees up, rather than remaining memory-resident for its entire extent.

## 4. Inlining

**Bottom-up vs. top-down inlining order with cost-benefit heuristics.** Inlining decisions are made by walking the call graph, typically bottom-up (callees inlined/finalized before their callers are processed) so that a caller's cost estimate already reflects any inlining done inside the callee, avoiding duplicated analysis. Each candidate call site is scored by a **cost-benefit heuristic**: estimated code-size growth (number of IR instructions added, weighted by block frequency) versus estimated benefit (eliminated call/return overhead, enabling of constant propagation when arguments are compile-time constants at the call site, and unlocking of downstream optimizations). Compilers impose a **size growth threshold** (e.g. LLVM's inline cost model producing a numeric threshold compared against an inlining cost budget that varies by optimization level and by whether the call site is in a hot region) and typically favor inlining very small functions unconditionally while gating larger ones behind profitability analysis.

**Profile-guided and speculative/guarded inlining.** With **profile-guided optimization (PGO)**, call-site edge frequencies from instrumented or sampled profiles bias the cost model toward inlining hot call sites even when static cost estimates are marginal, and away from inlining cold ones regardless of size. In managed-runtime JITs facing polymorphic dispatch, **inline caches** (monomorphic, polymorphic, and megamorphic, as popularized by Self and used in V8 and HotSpot) record the actually-observed receiver types at a call site at run time; when a site is monomorphic (one type ever observed), the JIT performs **speculative/guarded inlining**: it inlines the single observed target behind a cheap type guard, and if the guard fails at run time, it **deoptimizes** (bails out to an interpreter or less-optimized tier) rather than requiring the inlined code to handle all possible types. HotSpot's C2 and V8's TurboFan both rely on this guard-plus-deoptimization pattern pervasively; it lets them inline through virtual calls that a purely static whole-program analysis could not prove monomorphic.

**Partial inlining and recursion/budget control.** **Partial inlining** inlines only a function's cheap, frequently executed prefix (e.g. a fast-path check) at the call site while leaving a real call to the rest of the function for the cold path, reducing code growth while still removing call overhead on the hot path. For recursive or deeply nested call chains, compilers enforce a **budget-based worklist algorithm**: a global or per-function inlining budget is decremented as inlining proceeds, and recursive calls are capped by an explicit recursion-depth or duplication-factor limit to prevent unbounded code expansion. Inlining also interacts with alias and escape analysis: inlining a callee exposes its loads/stores and allocations directly in the caller's IR, which lets escape analysis prove an object passed into the (now-inlined) callee never escapes the caller, enabling stack allocation or scalar replacement that would have been invisible across an un-inlined call boundary — this cross-pass synergy is a primary reason inlining is scheduled early and iteratively in most optimization pipelines, despite its code-bloat cost.

## 5. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph-based escape analysis (Choi, Gupta, Serrano, Sreedhar, Midkiff).** This classical algorithm, used in Java JIT compilers, builds a **connection graph** per method: nodes represent abstract objects (one per allocation site) and local/field references, edges represent points-to and field-reference relationships, and each node is annotated with one of three escape states — **NoEscape** (never leaves the current method or thread), **ArgEscape** (passed as an argument, potentially escaping into a callee but not globally), or **GlobalEscape** (stored into a static field, a heap object reachable from outside, or returned and reachable afterward). The analysis propagates escape states along the connection graph edges (if an object pointed to by a field of an escaping object exists, it inherits at least that escape level) to a fixpoint, and the result directly gates the other mechanisms below.

**Scalar replacement of aggregates and stack allocation, enabled by NoEscape.** Once escape analysis proves an allocation site is NoEscape, two optimizations become sound: **stack allocation** (allocate the object on the stack frame instead of the heap, eliminating a GC-managed allocation entirely, valid because the object's lifetime provably doesn't outlive the frame), and more aggressively, **scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA)**, which eliminates the object's memory representation altogether and replaces each of its fields with independent scalar SSA values, as if the fields were ordinary local variables — this is only sound when the object doesn't escape and when all its uses are decomposable (no escaping references to the whole object, e.g. no pointer arithmetic over it or address-taken use that would require a real memory layout).

**Partial escape analysis (Stadler, Würthinger, Mössenböck, used in Graal/HotSpot).** Rather than a binary escape/no-escape classification per allocation site valid for the whole method, partial escape analysis performs this reasoning **per control-flow path**: an object may escape along some paths from its allocation point but not others (e.g. it escapes only inside a rarely taken branch that throws an exception or stores it globally). The analysis virtualizes the allocation (treats it as a set of scalar values, deferring actual materialization) along non-escaping paths and only **materializes** the real heap object lazily at the point where a path first causes it to escape, which recovers much of scalar replacement's benefit even for objects that are conditionally, rather than never, escaping.

**Synchronization elimination via thread-escape distinction.** A separate, coarser-grained analysis — **thread-escape analysis** — determines whether an object is ever made reachable from more than one thread, which is a weaker condition than full method/global escape. If an object is proven never to escape its allocating thread, any `synchronized` blocks or locks guarding access to it are provably uncontended and can undergo **lock elision** (removing the lock operations entirely) or **lock coarsening** (merging adjacent/nested lock acquisitions on the same provably-uncontended object into a single wider critical section), independent of whether the object also satisfies the stricter method-local NoEscape condition needed for stack allocation.

## 6. Loop Vectorization

**SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization vs. loop-level vectorization (Larsen & Amarasinghe).** Loop-level vectorization transforms a single loop's repeated scalar iterations into operations over vector registers (classic "loopy" vectorization: one logical operation applied across lanes corresponding to consecutive iterations). **SLP vectorization**, by contrast, operates within a basic block (or a small set of isomorphic statements) with no loop at all, packing multiple *independent scalar instructions* that perform the same operation on different data into a single SIMD instruction — e.g. four separate scalar additions on unrelated variables in straight-line code become one vector add. LLVM implements both as separate passes (the **Loop Vectorizer, LV**, and the **SLP vectorizer**), and they are often run in sequence because loop vectorization can leave behind straight-line remainder code that SLP can further pack.

**Dependence analysis for legality.** Before vectorizing, the compiler must prove the transformation doesn't reorder dependent memory accesses in a way that changes semantics. This uses classical **data dependence analysis**: representing array accesses across iterations with **distance vectors** and **direction vectors**, and testing for integer solutions to the dependence equations via the **GCD test** (a quick necessary-but-not-sufficient check based on the greatest common divisor of coefficients) or the more precise but costlier **Banerjee test** (bounding the existence of integer solutions within loop bounds) or the exact-but-expensive **Omega test** (an integer linear programming-based decision procedure) for more complex affine access patterns. A loop-carried dependence with a backward direction vector within the vectorization factor generally blocks vectorization unless the access pattern is provably safe (e.g. a reduction).

**If-conversion, masking/predication, and strip-mining.** Loops containing conditional control flow must first undergo **if-conversion**: branches are converted into **predicated/masked** operations (every vector lane computes its result, but a mask vector selects whether to commit it), turning control dependence into data dependence so the loop body becomes straight-line vector code. For loop trip counts not evenly divisible by the vectorization factor (VF), compilers generate a **remainder/epilogue loop** or use **masking for the final partial iteration** directly instead of a separate scalar tail. **Strip-mining** restructures the original loop into an outer loop stepping by the vector width and an inner "vector-body" loop/block executing VF elements at a time; a related modern technique is **vector-length-agnostic (VLA) vectorization** (as used by ARM SVE and RISC-V V extension codegen), where the generated code doesn't hardcode VF at compile time but queries the hardware vector length at run time, letting one binary run efficiently across different vector widths.

**Reduction recognition and cost modeling.** Operations like summation or max-accumulation across loop iterations are recognized as **reductions**: the compiler proves the accumulation operator is associative (and, if reordering is required, that reassociation is either safe or explicitly permitted, e.g. via a fast-math flag for floating-point sums where IEEE 754 addition isn't strictly associative) and vectorizes by accumulating into a vector of partial sums, horizontally reducing to a scalar only after the loop. Finally, a **cost model** chooses the actual vectorization factor and **interleave/unroll factor** by comparing estimated cycle cost of the vectorized code (accounting for target-specific vector instruction latencies, shuffle/permute overhead, and memory access patterns such as strided or gather/scatter loads) against the scalar baseline; LLVM's Loop Vectorizer explicitly enumerates several candidate VFs and interleave factors and picks the one with the lowest computed cost for the target architecture.

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling over a data-dependence DAG.** The compiler builds a **dependence DAG** per scheduling region (basic block, superblock, or larger) where nodes are instructions and edges encode **true dependencies (RAW — read-after-write)**, **anti-dependencies (WAR — write-after-read)**, and **output dependencies (WAW — write-after-write)**, each edge weighted by the latency of the producing instruction. **List scheduling** maintains a ready list of instructions whose predecessors are already scheduled and repeatedly picks the next instruction by a **priority function** — most commonly **critical-path priority** (schedule the instruction on the longest remaining latency-weighted path to the DAG's end first), sometimes combined with tie-breakers for register pressure or resource contention — while respecting a model of the target's **issue resources** (functional unit occupancy, issue width, pipeline hazards) so the scheduler doesn't issue more instructions of a given class per cycle than hardware supports.

**Trace scheduling (Fisher) for VLIW.** To schedule across basic block boundaries (necessary to fill the wide issue slots of VLIW machines), **trace scheduling** selects the most frequently executed path through a region (a "trace," typically chosen using profile data) spanning multiple basic blocks and schedules it as if it were a single block, moving instructions across the branches that were elided from the trace. Because instructions can migrate above or below side-entrances/side-exits from off-trace control flow, the algorithm must insert **compensation code** in the off-trace blocks to preserve correctness for the (less common) control paths that don't follow the selected trace — this compensation-code bookkeeping is the central complexity of trace scheduling compared to single-block list scheduling.

**Software pipelining / modulo scheduling (Lam).** For tight inner loops, **software pipelining** overlaps the execution of consecutive loop iterations so that, in steady state, instructions from several different original iterations execute concurrently, maximizing functional-unit utilization. **Modulo scheduling** (Lam's algorithm) is the standard formulation: it schedules one iteration's instructions into a repeating pattern with a fixed **initiation interval (II)** — the number of cycles between the start of successive iterations — chosen to be the smallest value satisfying two lower bounds: **ResMII** (resource-constrained minimum II, derived from the busiest functional unit's required throughput) and **RecMII** (recurrence-constrained minimum II, derived from the latency around the tightest dependence cycle in the loop body, since a loop-carried dependence chain bounds how fast iterations can start). The scheduler iteratively tries candidate IIs starting from max(ResMII, RecMII) and attempts to place instructions within a modulo reservation table, increasing II until a legal schedule is found; the result requires a **prologue** (ramp-up) and **epilogue** (ramp-down) around the pipelined steady-state kernel.

**Region and superblock scheduling for EPIC/VLIW, and phase-ordering with register allocation.** **Superblock scheduling** forms single-entry, multiple-exit regions by tail-duplicating code after branches (so a superblock has no side-entrances, simplifying the compensation-code problem relative to general trace scheduling) and schedules within that larger region, used heavily in EPIC architectures (e.g. Itanium) where the compiler, not hardware, is responsible for discovering instruction-level parallelism. A persistent cross-cutting issue is the **phase-ordering problem between scheduling and register allocation**: scheduling before allocation can discover more ILP but may increase live-range overlap and thus register pressure (causing spills), while allocating first fixes register pressure but can constrain the scheduler with artificial WAR/WAW false dependencies introduced by reusing the same physical register for unrelated values; production pipelines typically run a pre-allocation scheduling pass, then allocation, then a post-allocation scheduling pass to clean up the schedule given final register assignments.

## 8. Loop Optimizations (general)

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM).** Hoists computations whose operands don't change across loop iterations out of the loop body into the loop's preheader, so the computation executes once instead of per-iteration. Safety requires more than just operand invariance: the hoisted instruction must not have been **speculatively executed** in a way that introduces a trap/exception that wouldn't have occurred in the original program (e.g. hoisting a division that might divide by zero only on some iterations, or a load that might fault on an iteration that was never actually reached in the original control flow), so LICM typically requires the instruction to be either provably safe to speculate (no side effects, no possible trap) or guarded by the hoisted motion only reaching code that the original loop was guaranteed to execute at least once.

**Induction variable analysis and strength reduction.** The compiler recognizes **induction variables** — variables that vary by a fixed, loop-computable increment each iteration, classified as **basic induction variables** (directly incremented, e.g. `i = i + 1`) and **derived/linear induction variables** (computed as an affine function of a basic IV, e.g. `j = 4*i + 8`, often arising from array indexing/address computation). **Strength reduction** rewrites derived induction variables that involve multiplication into equivalent variables updated by addition alone (replacing `j = 4*i` recomputed each iteration with `j += 4` incrementally), eliminating expensive multiply operations from the loop body — the classic motivating case for this transformation historically was address computation for array accesses.

**Loop unrolling and unroll-and-jam.** **Loop unrolling** replicates the loop body k times per iteration of an outer control structure, reducing loop-overhead (branch and induction-variable-update instructions) as a fraction of total work and exposing more instructions for scheduling and other local optimizations across what were originally separate iterations. **Unroll-and-jam** applies this to a nested loop: the outer loop is unrolled, and the resulting multiple copies of the inner loop are then fused ("jammed") into a single inner loop, which increases opportunities for reuse of values loaded across what were originally different outer-loop iterations (improving cache locality and enabling further scalar optimization across the jammed bodies), subject to dependence constraints similar to those governing loop fusion.

**Loop fusion/fission (distribution) and loop interchange.** **Loop fusion** merges two adjacent loops with compatible bounds into one, amortizing loop overhead and improving locality when both loops touch the same data; it is legal only when no dependence from the second loop's body to the first (after fusion) would be reversed relative to program order, checked via dependence analysis on data accessed by both loops. **Loop fission (distribution)** is the inverse: splitting one loop into multiple loops, each handling part of the original body, useful when different parts have different vectorization/parallelization opportunities or when splitting breaks a dependence cycle that was blocking some other transformation. **Loop interchange** swaps the nesting order of two loops (e.g. making the inner loop the outer one) to improve memory locality, by arranging for the innermost loop to stride over the dimension contiguous in memory; its legality is determined from the dependence **direction vectors** of the loop nest, since interchange is illegal if it would reverse a dependence direction in a way that violates the original execution order (specifically, interchange is illegal in the presence of a dependence whose direction vector has a "<" in the position of the loop being moved outward after a ">" in an outer position, roughly — the precise rule is that the interchanged direction vector must not contain a "reversed" lexicographically negative dependence that wasn't satisfiable before interchange).

**Polyhedral loop transformations (the polyhedral model, affine scheduling, Pluto).** For loop nests with affine bounds and affine array-index expressions, the **polyhedral model** represents each statement's iteration space as a geometric polyhedron (points are iteration vectors satisfying the loop bounds as linear inequalities) and represents data dependences as affine relations between points in different statements' iteration spaces. Rather than applying discrete named transformations (fusion, interchange, tiling) one at a time, polyhedral compilation computes a new **affine scheduling function** directly — a linear map from old iteration vectors to new execution timestamps — that satisfies all dependence constraints while optimizing an objective. The **Pluto algorithm** is the standard practical instantiation: it formulates affine scheduling as an integer linear program whose objective simultaneously maximizes coarse-grained parallelism (by minimizing dependence distances across what become parallel loop dimensions) and improves data locality (by minimizing reuse distance, effectively achieving the combined effect of tiling, fusion, and interchange in one unified transformation), producing a schedule from which tiled, parallelized, locality-optimized code is regenerated via polyhedral code generation (e.g. CLooG-style scanning of the transformed polyhedron back into loop nests).

---

Answer: The brief above (Sections 1–8) delivers, for each requested area, at least three precisely named and technically detailed mechanisms: SSA construction (Cytron et al. dominance-frontier algorithm with Lengauer–Tarjan dominators, Braun et al.'s simple construction, SSA destruction/lost-copy-swap handling); alias analysis (Andersen's inclusion-based, Steensgaard's unification-based, type-based alias analysis, with flow/context/field-sensitivity axes); register allocation (Chaitin–Briggs graph coloring with optimistic coloring and conservative coalescing, linear scan with second-chance binpacking, SSA-based chordal-graph allocation, plus live-range splitting and rematerialization); inlining (bottom-up cost-benefit heuristics with PGO, speculative/guarded inlining via inline caches and deoptimization, partial inlining and budget-based recursion limits); escape analysis (Choi et al. connection-graph analysis, scalar replacement/stack allocation, Stadler et al. partial escape analysis, thread-escape-based lock elision/coarsening); loop vectorization (SLP vs. loop-level vectorization, dependence analysis via GCD/Banerjee/Omega tests, if-conversion/masking/strip-mining/VLA vectorization, reduction recognition and cost modeling); instruction scheduling (list scheduling with critical-path priority over dependence DAGs, trace scheduling with compensation code, modulo scheduling via ResMII/RecMII, superblock scheduling and the scheduling/register-allocation phase-ordering problem); and loop optimizations (LICM with speculation-safety conditions, induction variable analysis with strength reduction, unrolling/unroll-and-jam, fusion/fission/interchange governed by dependence direction vectors, and polyhedral/Pluto affine scheduling).

response.content:
# Technical Brief: SSA Construction, Alias Analysis, and Escape Analysis

## 1. SSA Construction

### 1.1 Dominance, dominator trees, and the Lengauer-Tarjan algorithm

Static single assignment form requires that every variable have exactly one static definition and that every use be dominated by its definition. Node `d` dominates node `n` if every control-flow path from the entry to `n` passes through `d`. The dominator tree encodes the immediate dominator (`idom`) relation: `idom(n)` is the unique closest strict dominator of `n`, and the tree's edges are `idom` edges.

The classical algorithm for computing dominators efficiently is **Lengauer-Tarjan**, which runs in O(E log V) (the near-linear variant with a more sophisticated path-compression/link-eval structure approaches O(E α(E,V))). It operates on a depth-first spanning tree of the CFG, computing *semidominators* via DFS numbering and a union-find-like structure over the DFS tree, then correcting semidominators into true immediate dominators in a second pass using the semidominator theorem. In practice, many production compilers (LLVM included) instead use the simpler iterative **Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy** dataflow algorithm, which computes dominators via repeated meet-over-predecessors (`idom(n) = intersect of idom(p) for p in preds(n)`) to a fixpoint using a reverse-postorder traversal; it is easier to implement and nearly as fast in practice despite worse theoretical complexity, because CFGs are close to reducible and converge in few iterations.

### 1.2 Dominance frontiers and the Cytron-Ferrante-Rosen-Wegman-Zadeck (CFRWZ) algorithm

The **dominance frontier** of a node `n`, DF(n), is the set of nodes `m` such that `n` dominates a predecessor of `m` but `n` does not strictly dominate `m` itself. Intuitively, DF(n) is where `n`'s dominance "runs out" — the first merge points reachable from `n` where control-flow paths that did and didn't pass through `n` reconverge. This is precisely where a phi-node may be needed for any variable defined at `n`.

CFRWZ compute dominance frontiers efficiently using the dominator tree via a bottom-up traversal:
- For each node `n`, iterate its CFG successors `s`. If `idom(s) != n`, then `s ∈ DF(n)` (a "local" contribution — join points immediately reachable).
- Then propagate "up" the dominator tree: for each child `c` of `n` in the dominator tree, for each `w ∈ DF(c)`, if `n` does not strictly dominate `w`, add `w` to DF(n) (the "DF-up" contribution).

This yields DF(n) for all n in roughly O(V²) worst case but near-linear in practice for typical CFGs.

**Phi placement** uses the iterated dominance frontier (IDF): for a variable `v` with definition sites `Defs(v)`, the minimal set of join points needing phi-nodes is the closure of DF over Defs(v) — i.e., DF⁺(Defs(v)) = DF(Defs(v)) ∪ DF(DF(Defs(v))) ∪ ... until fixpoint. The standard worklist algorithm pushes all definition blocks, and for each block popped, inserts a phi for `v` at every node in its dominance frontier not already having one, pushing newly-phi'd nodes onto the worklist (since inserting a phi counts as a new "definition" of `v` for iteration purposes).

This placement is **correct**: every use of `v` not dominated by a single definition is guaranteed to be reachable from a join point carrying a phi. It is not automatically **minimal** in the SSA-minimality sense (no redundant phis) without pruning — this motivates semi-pruned/pruned SSA.

### 1.3 Semi-pruned, pruned, and minimal SSA

Naively computing IDF for every variable and inserting phis for all of them produces correct but bloated SSA, since local variables never live across blocks don't need any phis. Three refinement levels are standard:

- **Unpruned SSA**: phi insertion based purely on IDF of raw assignment sites, ignoring liveness; phis get inserted even for dead/non-live variables.
- **Semi-pruned SSA**: a cheap pre-pass computes which variables are *live-across a basic block boundary at all* (a crude global-ness test, not full liveness) and excludes purely-local variables from phi insertion entirely. This eliminates most unnecessary phis cheaply without running full liveness analysis.
- **Pruned SSA**: phis are inserted only where the variable is actually *live* at that join point, using full liveness analysis (live-in sets). This yields the minimal phi placement with respect to liveness — no phi exists at a point where its result is dead.
- **Minimal SSA** (CFRWZ's original formal property) refers to a placement where the number of phi functions is the theoretical minimum needed for correctness assuming every definition is potentially live — i.e., exactly the IDF set, without considering liveness. Minimal SSA can still contain phis for dead values; pruned SSA additionally removes those. Most production compilers target pruned SSA, since it is both minimal in placement and liveness-driven.

### 1.4 Renaming via the dominator-tree variable-versioning stack algorithm

After phi placement, the **renaming pass** assigns each definition a fresh SSA version and rewrites uses to reference the version reaching them, using the dominator tree structure. A per-original-variable stack of current versions is maintained; the algorithm does a preorder DFS over the dominator tree:

1. On entering block `n`: for each phi in `n`, push a new version as the phi's definition.
2. Process `n`'s statements in order: rewrite each use by peeking the top of the corresponding variable's stack; for each def, push a fresh version.
3. For each CFG successor `s` of `n` that has a phi for variable `v`, fill in the phi operand corresponding to edge `(n,s)` with the current top-of-stack version of `v`.
4. Recurse into dominator-tree children of `n`.
5. On exiting `n`, pop all versions pushed while processing `n` (restoring the stack to its pre-entry state).

This works correctly because dominator-tree preorder guarantees that when processing `n`, the top of each stack is exactly the version of that variable from the definition that dominates `n` — which is precisely the SSA dominance property required.

### 1.5 Braun et al.'s simple/efficient construction

**Braun, Buchwald, Hack, Leißa, Mallon, Zwinkau (C 2013)** present a single-pass alternative avoiding explicit dominance-frontier computation. Values are looked up recursively per-block (`readVariable`), building phis on demand at block entry when a value isn't locally available:
- If the block has a known single predecessor, recurse into it (this is local value numbering extended across trivial CFG edges).
- If the block has multiple predecessors, optimistically insert an incomplete/empty phi first (to break cycles in loops), recursively query each predecessor, and fill in phi operands.
- Blocks not yet sealed (not all predecessors known, e.g., mid-construction of a loop header before the back edge is added) defer phi operand resolution until sealing.

This produces **non-minimal** SSA in general (redundant phis, e.g., all-same-operand phis), so a cleanup pass is applied: **trivial phi removal** — any phi whose operands are all equal (or all the phi itself, i.e., self-referential) is replaced by that single value, recursively (since removing one phi can trivialize another that used it). This optimistic-insert-then-simplify strategy achieves SSA minimality equivalent to CFRWZ's IDF-based result without ever materializing the dominator tree or dominance frontiers explicitly, at the cost of needing the recursive simplification pass and careful handling of unsealed blocks for loops.

### 1.6 SSA destruction

Converting back to non-SSA form ("phi elimination") must replace each phi with ordinary copy instructions on each predecessor edge, but naive copy insertion is unsound in the presence of parallel/concurrent semantics of phi operands. Two canonical pathologies:

- **Lost-copy problem**: if a value used by a phi is overwritten by another copy inserted for a *different* phi on the same edge before the first copy executes, the original value is lost. This arises because phi operand assignments on a given predecessor edge are logically simultaneous (parallel copies) but get sequentialized.
- **Swap problem**: two phis mutually exchange values along the same edge (`x = phi(y,...); y = phi(x,...)`), which sequential copies cannot express without a temporary — a sequential copy `x := y; y := x` destroys the needed simultaneity, requiring a true swap or temp register.

**Sreedhar, Gao, et al.**'s approach fixes this via **live-range splitting**: instead of emitting copies naively, each phi's operand is first copied into a fresh temporary at the *end of the corresponding predecessor block*, and the phi's result is copied from a fresh temporary at the *start of the block containing the phi*. This decouples the "parallel copy problem" into a sequence of ordinary copies that provably cannot exhibit lost-copy or swap pathologies, because all interference is resolved by the extra temporaries — effectively treating the simultaneous phi-operand assignment as a parallel-copy instruction which is then correctly sequentialized (topologically, inserting swaps/temps only where real cyclic interference exists, e.g. in register-allocated code where copies alias physical locations).

---

## 2. Alias Analysis

### 2.1 Andersen's inclusion-based (subset-constraint) analysis

**Andersen's analysis** models each variable/location `p` with a points-to set `pts(p)`, and models the program as a system of set-inclusion constraints:
- `p = &q` ⟹ `q ∈ pts(p)`
- `p = q` ⟹ `pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)`
- `p = *q` ⟹ for all `a ∈ pts(q)`, `pts(a) ⊆ pts(p)`
- `*p = q` ⟹ for all `a ∈ pts(p)`, `pts(q) ⊆ pts(a)`

This is solved to a least fixpoint by iterative constraint propagation (worklist-based), equivalent to computing reachability in a constraint graph where dereference constraints dynamically add new subset edges as points-to sets grow. Complexity is **O(n³)** in the worst case (cubic in program size) because each of O(n²) possible points-to edges can trigger O(n) propagation steps; practical implementations use techniques like offline variable substitution, cycle elimination, and bitvector/BDD-based set representations (e.g., `bddbddb`) to scale. Andersen's is **flow-insensitive** (a single points-to set per variable for the whole program, ignoring program order) and **context-insensitive** in its basic form, but is the most precise widely-used points-to formulation because it tracks subset relationships rather than collapsing them.

### 2.2 Steensgaard's unification-based analysis

**Steensgaard's analysis** instead unifies points-to information: whenever two pointers are assigned to each other, their abstract storage locations are *merged* (union-find) rather than linked by a subset edge. This models constraints with equality instead of inclusion, so each abstract location has at most one outgoing "points-to" edge at any time (a function from locations to locations, effectively a type-like structure). This yields **near-linear time**, O(n α(n)) with union-find, since there's no need to repeatedly propagate subset growth — one pass of unification suffices (modulo iterating to fixpoint for cyclic structures, which still converges quickly). The cost is substantial precision loss: merging destroys the distinction between "p may point to a or b" in the inclusion sense, often causing many unrelated pointers to collapse into one equivalence class after a single unifying assignment. This is the standard "fast but imprecise vs. slow but precise" alias-analysis tradeoff point of reference.

### 2.3 Type-based alias analysis (TBAA)

**TBAA**, used in LLVM and GCC's `-fstrict-aliasing`, derives non-aliasing information from the source language's type system rather than from pointer-flow constraints. In C/C++, the strict aliasing rule states that an object may only be accessed through an lvalue of a compatible type (modulo `char*`/similar exceptions), so the compiler assumes two pointers of incompatible types never alias. LLVM implements this via `!tbaa` metadata attached to load/store instructions, encoding a type tree (base type, access path/offset, and size) built from the source language's type hierarchy; alias queries compare these metadata nodes using structural/tree-based compatibility rules (ancestor relationships in the type DAG) rather than any points-to computation. TBAA is cheap (metadata lookup, no fixpoint computation) but unsound in the presence of type-punning/undefined-behavior-adjacent code, which is the classic source of `-fno-strict-aliasing` bug reports.

### 2.4 Sensitivity axes and the alias lattice

Alias analyses are classified along independent axes:
- **Flow-sensitivity**: flow-sensitive analyses compute distinct points-to sets per program point (precise but expensive, essentially a dataflow analysis); flow-insensitive analyses compute one summary set per variable valid at all points (cheaper, standard for whole-program Andersen/Steensgaard).
- **Context-sensitivity**: context-insensitive analysis merges information across all call sites of a function; context-sensitive analysis distinguishes calling contexts, via mechanisms like **call-strings** (k-CFA: track the last k call sites on the stack as part of the abstract state, bounding context depth) or **functional/summary-based** approaches (computing a function summary parameterized by input points-to state, as in Whaley/Lam's BDD-based context-sensitive Andersen's). k-CFA with k=0 degenerates to context-insensitivity; higher k trades precision for an exponential blowup in context count.
- **Field-sensitivity**: field-sensitive analysis distinguishes individual struct/object fields (`p->a` vs `p->b` as separate abstract locations); field-insensitive analysis collapses an entire aggregate into one location, causing spurious aliasing between unrelated fields.
- **Heap modeling**: allocation-site-based abstraction (one abstract object per static `malloc`/`new` call site, possibly merging all dynamic instances) is standard; more precise variants use shape analysis or recency abstraction to distinguish the most-recently-allocated object from older ones at the same site.

LLVM's alias analysis results are expressed on a **lattice** with four outcomes for a pair of memory accesses: **MustAlias** (always refer to the same location), **NoAlias** (never overlap), **MayAlias** (unknown/conservative — may or may not overlap), and **PartialAlias** (overlap but not identically, e.g., accessing different offsets within the same object). These results flow into optimizations like load/store reordering, redundant load elimination, and vectorization legality checks, where NoAlias licenses the most aggressive transformations and MayAlias forces conservative ordering.

---

## 3. Escape Analysis

### 3.1 Connection-graph-based escape analysis (Choi, Gupta, Serrano, Sreedhar, Midkiff)

The canonical algorithm, used in IBM's Java JIT and influential on HotSpot's implementation, builds a **connection graph** per method: nodes represent object abstractions (allocation sites, formal parameters, return values, "phantom" nodes for unknown external objects) and *field edges* / *points-to edges* represent reference relationships discovered via a flow-sensitive, intraprocedural (then interprocedurally summarized) analysis of the method's statements. Each node is labeled with an **escape state**:
- **NoEscape**: object is only reachable from within the current method/thread-local context, never stored into a field of another object or returned, and never passed where it could become visible outside.
- **ArgEscape**: object escapes only by being passed as a call argument but does not escape to the heap/global scope beyond that call (a refinement letting some interprocedural reasoning remain tractable without inlining).
- **GlobalEscape**: object is stored into a static field, a heap object reachable from outside the method, or returned, making it potentially visible to arbitrary other threads/methods.

The connection graph is built bottom-up: for each call site, a parameterized summary of the callee's connection graph is spliced into the caller's graph (mapping callee formal-parameter nodes to the actual argument nodes at the call site), avoiding full inlining while still propagating escape information interprocedurally. Escape states propagate via graph reachability from "escaping" roots (static fields, thread objects, return edges) backward to allocation-site nodes.

### 3.2 Escape analysis via points-to/alias analysis reuse

A simpler engineering approach treats escape analysis as a derived query over an existing points-to analysis (e.g., Andersen's-style): an allocation site "escapes" if its corresponding abstract object node is reachable, in the points-to graph, from any location considered externally visible (global variables, heap fields, return values, thread-escaping structures). This reuses the same constraint-based machinery already built for alias analysis, trading some precision (points-to analysis is typically context- and flow-insensitive, so escape conclusions are correspondingly coarser) for implementation simplicity and shared infrastructure — common in ahead-of-time/whole-program compilers (e.g., some escape analyses in Go's compiler effectively perform a flow-sensitive, intraprocedural variant of this idea extended with explicit call-graph-based interprocedural escape propagation).

### 3.3 Partial escape analysis (Stadler, Würthinger, Mössenböck — Graal/HotSpot)

Classical escape analysis is a static, binary, whole-method property: an object either escapes (no optimization) or doesn't (fully optimizable). **Partial escape analysis**, implemented in Graal, instead performs escape analysis *on a control-flow-sensitive basis within the method*, tracking "virtual" (not-yet-materialized) objects along each control-flow path independently. An object can remain virtual (scalar-replaced, not allocated) along paths where it never escapes, and only get **materialized** (actually allocated on the heap) lazily at the specific point along a particular control-flow path where it first escapes (e.g., stored into a field or passed to a call that isn't inlined), rather than being pessimistically allocated at the original allocation site just because *some* path escapes. This works via an abstract interpretation over an extended value lattice containing "virtual object" states, merging at control-flow join points (materializing if the virtual-object states disagree across incoming paths) and is integrated with speculative/optimistic compilation and deoptimization (if runtime behavior diverges from the speculated non-escaping assumption).

### 3.4 Scalar replacement of aggregates, stack allocation, and synchronization elimination

Escape analysis is a precondition enabling several concrete transformations:

- **Scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA)**: if an object is proven non-escaping (or partially non-escaping along a region), its fields can be replaced by independent scalar SSA values, eliminating the heap object entirely and letting field accesses become register/SSA-value operations subject to further standard scalar optimization (constant propagation, dead code elimination) — this is the dominant payoff of escape analysis in JIT compilers.
- **Stack allocation**: when SROA isn't fully applicable (e.g., the object's address is taken but doesn't outlive the frame) a non-escaping object can still be allocated on the stack frame rather than the heap, avoiding GC pressure and allocation overhead while preserving identity/addressability.
- **Synchronization elimination**: a distinct dimension, **thread-escape analysis**, determines whether an object is ever reachable by more than one thread (as opposed to method-escape analysis, which asks whether an object outlives its allocating method's frame). An object that is method-escaping (e.g., returned or stored in a field) can still be thread-local if no other thread can ever obtain a reference to it; in that case, `synchronized` blocks/monitor operations on that object are provably uncontended and can be eliminated entirely (lock elision) or, when only some call paths are thread-shared, coarsened by merging adjacent lock/unlock pairs into a single critical section (lock coarsening) to amortize locking overhead. This requires its own escape lattice (thread-local / thread-shared) layered on top of, but conceptually orthogonal to, the heap/method-escape classification used for allocation decisions.

# Technical Brief: Register Allocation and Instruction Scheduling

## 1. Register Allocation

### 1.1 Graph-Coloring Register Allocation (Chaitin-Briggs)

The classical formulation, due to Chaitin et al. (1981) and refined by Briggs et al. (1994), models register allocation as graph coloring. The compiler builds an **interference graph** G = (V, E) where V is the set of live ranges (or webs — maximal unions of def-use chains connected by shared variables) and an edge (a, b) ∈ E exists iff a and b are simultaneously live at some program point and cannot occupy the same register. Interference graph construction requires prior **liveness analysis** (a backward dataflow analysis computing LiveIn/LiveOut sets at each program point); two live ranges interfere if one is live-out of a definition point for the other, or more precisely, at any point both are in the LiveOut set and distinct.

A k-coloring of G (k = number of physical registers) exists iff G can be colored such that no two adjacent nodes share a color. Graph coloring is NP-complete in general (reduction from the classical k-colorability decision problem), so allocators use heuristics rather than exact algorithms.

**Chaitin's algorithm** uses a simplify/spill worklist:
- **Simplify**: repeatedly remove any node with degree < k from the graph, pushing it onto a stack. Such nodes are trivially colorable later because fewer than k neighbors can possibly conflict.
- **Spill**: if no node has degree < k, the algorithm is stuck. Chaitin's original approach picks a node (via a spill cost heuristic) and marks it for spilling optimistically — removing it from the graph on the assumption it will not need a color, without actually guaranteeing success.
- **Select**: pop nodes off the stack and assign colors greedily from the available palette, skipping colors used by already-colored neighbors.

**Briggs's optimistic coloring** modifies this: rather than treating a node pushed during a "spill" decision as permanently spilled, it is pushed onto the stack anyway (since degree ≥ k does not guarantee uncolorability — a node's k or more neighbors might not all receive distinct colors). The final color assignment is attempted during select, and only if no free color remains is the node actually spilled. This is strictly better than Chaitin's pessimistic approach because it discovers colorability that pure degree-based reasoning would miss.

**Spill cost heuristics**: when a node must be chosen for potential spilling, common cost functions estimate `cost(v) = Σ (spill_store_cost + spill_load_cost) × 10^loop_depth / degree(v)`, favoring spilling long, low-degree-adjusted, loop-infrequent live ranges over short, high-use-density ones. The division by degree (or degree²) biases toward spilling live ranges that will most reduce graph density per unit of inserted spill cost.

**Coalescing** merges live ranges connected by a copy/move instruction when they don't interfere, eliminating the move entirely (register-register move elision). This is essential because SSA construction and lowering introduce many copies (e.g., at phi nodes).
- **Chaitin's aggressive coalescing** merges any non-interfering copy-related pair immediately. This is effective at removing moves but can increase the degree of the merged node, potentially making the graph harder to k-color and inducing more spills.
- **Briggs's conservative coalescing** only merges two nodes a, b if the resulting merged node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k (the "Briggs test"), guaranteeing simplification is not impeded.
- **George's conservative coalescing** (a variant used in the Chaitin-Briggs-George iterated register coalescing framework) requires every neighbor of a to either already interfere with b or have degree < k — a different sufficient condition, often combined with Briggs's test in **iterated register coalescing (George & Appel, 1996)**, which interleaves simplify, coalesce, freeze, and spill worklists to avoid coalescing too early or too late.

**Spill code generation**: once a node is actually spilled, the allocator rewrites the program to insert a store after each definition and a load before each use of that value, typically using a fresh stack slot; the rewritten program is then re-colored (the whole simplify-select pipeline reruns), since spilling changes the interference graph. This may iterate to a fixed point.

**Live-range splitting** breaks one live range into multiple smaller, disjoint sub-ranges connected by copies, each independently colorable. This is used both to reduce interference graph density (splitting at loop boundaries, around calls, or at "hot"/"cold" boundaries) and in modern allocators (e.g., LLVM's greedy allocator) as an alternative to naive spilling — splitting a range so only the "cold" piece is spilled while the "hot" piece keeps a register.

**Rematerialization** avoids a reload by instead recomputing a value from scratch (e.g., reloading a constant via an immediate-load instruction rather than a memory load), when the recomputation is cheaper than a spill slot round-trip and the operands needed to recompute are still available. This requires marking certain defs as "rematerializable" (constants, simple address computations) during spill cost analysis.

### 1.2 Linear Scan Register Allocation

Linear scan (Poletto & Sarkar, 1999) trades optimality for speed, making it standard in JIT compilers (early V8's Crankshaft, the original LLVM JIT/fast register allocator, early HotSpot C1) where compilation latency dominates.

The algorithm first computes **live intervals**: for each virtual register, a (possibly non-contiguous, but commonly approximated as contiguous) range [start, end] over a linearized instruction numbering, derived from liveness analysis performed over a single linear ordering of the code (rather than full dataflow over a CFG, though CFG-aware variants exist for loops). Live intervals are sorted by increasing start point.

The core loop scans intervals in order, maintaining an **active set** of intervals currently assigned physical registers. For each new interval:
1. Expire intervals in the active set whose end point precedes the new interval's start, freeing their registers.
2. If a free register exists, assign it and add the interval to the active set.
3. If no register is free, select a victim to spill — typically the active interval with the **furthest end point** (Poletto-Sarkar's heuristic), on the grounds that spilling it frees a register for the longest remaining duration, minimizing total spill count.

This runs in O(n log n) (dominated by sorting), versus the iterative, potentially multi-pass nature of graph coloring, which is why it's favored under JIT time budgets despite producing measurably more spills on average.

**Second-chance binpacking** (used in e.g. the LuaJIT and some LLVM fast-allocator-style schemes, formalized by Traub, Holloway, Smith and extended by Wimmer & Mössenböck for SSA-based linear scan in the Java HotSpot client compiler) improves on vanilla linear scan by allowing a spilled interval to be **reloaded into a (possibly different) register later**, rather than being spilled for its entire remaining lifetime. The live interval is split at the spill point into multiple sub-intervals; each sub-interval gets its own register-assignment decision, essentially giving a spilled value a "second chance" to resume living in a register if one frees up downstream. This is a restricted, efficient form of live-range splitting integrated directly into the linear-scan pass, avoiding full graph-coloring overhead while still curbing spill-induced reload traffic.

### 1.3 SSA-Based Register Allocation (Chordal Graph Coloring)

Hack, Grund, and Goos (and independently Brisk et al.) observed that if a program is in **strict SSA form**, the interference graph of its live ranges is **chordal** (every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord). This follows from the tree-structured dominance relationships SSA imposes: live ranges of SSA values form intervals over the dominator tree, and dominance-based interval graphs are provably chordal.

Chordal graphs are **colorable in polynomial time** — specifically, a **perfect elimination ordering** (obtainable via **maximum cardinality search**, running in O(V + E)) allows a greedy coloring pass to find an optimal (minimum-color) coloring in linear/near-linear time, in sharp contrast to general graph coloring's NP-completeness. This means SSA-based allocators can find a provably minimal-register coloring for the "virtual" portion of allocation without heuristic simplify/spill/select iteration — spilling becomes a separate, principled pre-pass (deciding what to keep "in registers" before coloring) rather than an ad hoc fallback discovered mid-coloring.

Because this approach operates directly on SSA values, phi nodes at CFG merge points must be resolved post-coloring: this is the **"out-of-SSA" / SSA elimination** step, which inserts copy instructions along CFG edges to implement the phi semantics. When multiple SSA values must be permuted between registers (e.g., swapping the contents of two registers because each phi operand must land in the other's slot), this becomes a **parallel copy / permutation problem**, solved via **"puzzle solving"**: treating each register as a puzzle tile and the needed permutation as a cyclic rearrangement, resolved using a scratch register or an XOR-swap/cyclic-rotation sequence to implement the permutation with minimal extra moves. This puzzle-solving step is the chordal-SSA allocator's analog to coalescing in Chaitin-Briggs.

### 1.4 Summary Comparison

Graph-coloring (Chaitin-Briggs) gives strong spill quality via iterative refinement but at higher compile-time cost and heuristic (non-optimal) worst cases due to NP-completeness. Linear scan sacrifices spill quality for near-linear compile time, suited to JIT latency budgets, with second-chance binpacking narrowing the quality gap via targeted live-range splitting. SSA-chordal allocation achieves polynomial-time *optimal* coloring for a fixed spill set by exploiting SSA's chordal structure, pushing the hard combinatorial problem (what to spill) into a separable pre-pass, at the cost of requiring an explicit SSA-elimination/copy-insertion phase.

---

## 2. Instruction Scheduling

### 2.1 Data Dependence DAG Construction

All scheduling mechanisms operate over a **data dependence graph (DDG)**, a DAG whose nodes are instructions within a scheduling region and whose edges encode ordering constraints:
- **True dependence (RAW, read-after-write, "flow dependence")**: instruction j reads a value instruction i writes; i must execute before j.
- **Anti-dependence (WAR, write-after-read)**: instruction j writes a location instruction i reads; j must not execute before i reads it. This is a false dependence induced by register/memory reuse, not actual data flow, and can often be eliminated by renaming (replacing with a fresh register).
- **Output dependence (WAW, write-after-write)**: instruction j writes a location instruction i also writes; order must be preserved so the final value matches program semantics. Also eliminable by renaming in many cases.
- **Control dependences** anchor instructions to the branches that guard their execution, constraining which instructions may move across branch boundaries.

Each DAG edge is also annotated with a **latency**, the minimum number of cycles that must elapse between the issue of the source and sink instructions (e.g., multi-cycle multiply/load latencies, load-use delay slots). The scheduler's job is to find a topological order of the DAG, respecting these latencies, that minimizes a cost metric — typically total schedule length or critical-path completion time — subject to **resource constraints** modeling the target's functional units, issue width, and pipeline structure (e.g., only one load/store port, at most N instructions issued per cycle, reservation-table conflicts for multi-cycle pipelined units).

### 2.2 List Scheduling

**List scheduling** is the workhorse local scheduling algorithm. Given the DDG for a basic block (or scheduling region), it maintains a **ready list** of instructions whose predecessors have already been scheduled (and whose latencies have elapsed), and at each cycle greedily selects the highest-priority ready instruction(s) up to the issue-width limit, simulating resource usage via a resource-reservation table.

Priority functions determine schedule quality:
- **Critical-path priority**: prioritize instructions with the longest latency-weighted path to the DAG's exit node(s) (i.e., maximum remaining work), since delaying them risks lengthening the overall schedule.
- **Longest-latency-first**: among ready instructions, prefer high-latency operations (loads, multiplies) early so their results are available by the time dependents need them, hiding latency behind other work.
- Secondary tiebreakers include node height, number of successors, and register pressure effects (preferring to schedule instructions that free live ranges sooner, to ease downstream register allocation).

**Local list scheduling** operates within a single basic block. **Global list scheduling** extends the ready-list framework across block boundaries — into superblocks, regions, or the whole function — allowing instructions to move speculatively above or below branches, subject to correctness constraints enforced via compensation code.

### 2.3 Trace Scheduling (Fisher)

**Trace scheduling**, introduced by Joseph Fisher for early VLIW machines, selects a **trace** — a single most-likely linear path through the CFG (predicted via profile data or heuristics), potentially spanning multiple basic blocks and crossing conditional branches — and schedules it as if it were one large basic block, exposing maximal ILP for VLIW's wide, statically-scheduled issue slots.

Because the trace assumes a particular branch outcome at each conditional, instructions may be hoisted above a branch into positions the off-trace path doesn't expect, or sunk below a branch merge point. This requires **compensation code**: when control exits the trace off the predicted path (the branch is mispredicted relative to the trace), duplicate instructions must be inserted on the off-trace edges to restore correct semantics — e.g., if an instruction was speculatively hoisted above a branch under the assumption the branch is taken, the off-taken (not-taken) path must get a compensating copy of that instruction, since it didn't "see" the hoisted effect. Compensation code grows with the aggressiveness of hoisting and the number of off-trace exits, and poor trace selection (low prediction accuracy) can cause substantial code bloat and redundant computation on frequently-taken off-trace paths.

### 2.4 Software Pipelining and Modulo Scheduling

**Software pipelining** targets loops, overlapping iterations so that the steady state executes instructions from multiple successive logical iterations concurrently, analogous to hardware pipelining but done statically by the compiler.

**Modulo scheduling**, with **Lam's algorithm** (Monica Lam, 1988) as the canonical formulation, schedules one iteration's instructions into a compact kernel of length II (the **initiation interval**), such that successive iterations are issued II cycles apart, repeating the same relative schedule modulo II. The **steady-state kernel** is surrounded by a **prologue** (ramp-up, filling the pipeline with partial iterations) and **epilogue** (ramp-down, draining it).

The **minimum initiation interval (MII)** lower-bounds II and is computed as `MII = max(ResMII, RecMII)`:
- **ResMII (resource-constrained MII)**: for each resource (functional unit, issue slot), `ResMII ≥ ⌈(uses of that resource per iteration) / (available units of that resource)⌉`; ResMII is the max over all resources.
- **RecMII (recurrence-constrained MII)**: for each cycle in the dependence graph (a "recurrence," e.g., a loop-carried dependency like an accumulator update), `RecMII ≥ ⌈(sum of latencies around the cycle) / (distance of the cycle, i.e., number of iterations it spans)⌉`; RecMII is the max over all recurrence cycles. This reflects that a loop-carried dependence chain fundamentally limits how fast iterations can be re-initiated regardless of resource availability.

Lam's algorithm attempts scheduling at II = MII; if no valid modulo schedule is found (a slot conflict modulo II arises, i.e., **modulo resource conflict**), II is incremented and scheduling is retried, iterating until success (a technique often called **modulo scheduling with iterative II search**). Register allocation for pipelined loops introduces its own complication: because multiple iterations' live ranges overlap in the kernel, a value live across iteration boundaries needs multiple physical registers (one per overlapping iteration) unless **rotating register files** (as in Itanium/IA-64's EPIC architecture) are available to automatically re-map a logical register name across iterations without explicit renaming code.

### 2.5 Region and Superblock Scheduling (VLIW/EPIC)

**Superblock scheduling** forms single-entry, multiple-exit regions by **tail duplication**: whenever a trace or region would otherwise merge back with another path (multiple entries), the merging tail is duplicated per predecessor so the resulting region has only one entry point, simplifying scheduling (no need to handle joins mid-region) at the cost of code size growth. This is the dominant region-formation technique in EPIC compilers like the Itanium/IA-64 toolchain and many VLIW DSP compilers, because single-entry regions avoid trace scheduling's complex compensation-code bookkeeping for join points, while multiple-exit (branch-out) handling remains comparatively simple (just duplicate off-path instructions on exit edges if hoisted past the exit branch).

**Region scheduling** generalizes this to arbitrary acyclic subgraphs of the CFG (not necessarily linear traces), using techniques like **percolation scheduling** to move instructions upward across multiple control-flow paths simultaneously, guarded by predicates in architectures supporting predicated execution — letting the EPIC compiler expose ILP across branches without physically duplicating code, since predication subsumes some of what compensation code would otherwise require.

### 2.6 Resource Modeling for Pipelined/Superscalar Issue

Both list and modulo scheduling rely on an explicit **resource usage model**, typically a **reservation table**: a 2D grid (resource × relative cycle offset) describing which functional units/ports an instruction occupies at each cycle of its execution (not just its issue cycle, since pipelined multi-cycle units may hold a resource for several cycles, e.g., a non-pipelined divider). Scheduling legality requires that summing reservation tables for all co-scheduled instructions never exceeds unit capacity at any (resource, cycle) pair. Superscalar/VLIW issue-width constraints are modeled as a distinguished "issue slot" resource with capacity equal to the machine's issue width per cycle.

### 2.7 Phase-Ordering Interaction with Register Allocation

Instruction scheduling and register allocation have an inherent **phase-ordering problem**: scheduling before allocation can increase register pressure (moving independent instructions closer together to exploit ILP tends to widen the live ranges that must be simultaneously held, since more values are "in flight" at once), while allocating before scheduling fixes physical register assignments that constrain the scheduler's freedom to reorder (false dependencies — WAR/WAW — are introduced by register reuse that pure dataflow wouldn't require) and can block otherwise-exploitable ILP.

Common mitigations include: **pre-pass scheduling** (schedule first for ILP, accept higher pressure, let the allocator spill if needed) followed by **post-pass scheduling** (a second scheduling pass after allocation to clean up stalls introduced by spill code and to re-order around the register assignment's induced anti/output dependences); **integrated/combined approaches** that model register-pressure estimates directly in the scheduler's priority function (penalizing moves that increase live-range overlap); and, in SSA-based pipelines, deferring physical allocation until after an SSA-aware scheduling pass so that false WAR/WAW dependences (an artifact of physical register reuse) simply don't exist yet during scheduling, sidestepping much of the conflict. No universal ordering dominates; production compilers (e.g., LLVM's MachineScheduler running both pre-RA and post-RA passes) typically run scheduling twice, bracketing register allocation, to capture benefits of both orderings.
